question: The European Union is highly dependent on imports of soya for the production of feed for the livestock sector. Currently, around 66 % of the EU's plant protein needs comes from imports.

This strategic vulnerability is being amplified by geopolitical tensions, international trade constraints and recent events such as China’s suspension of Brazilian soybean imports due to pesticide contamination, which may lead to increased volatility on the global markets.

At the same time, the EU is seeking to reduce the climate footprint of the agri-food sector and support farmers in the transition to sustainable practices, while Europe’s protein and oilseed crop potential remains underexploited. Strengthening strategic autonomy in plant proteins is key to maintaining food security, farmers’ competitiveness and the resilience of European supply chains.

What measures is the Commission proposing to significantly boost internal production of protein and oilseed crops – such as soya, peas, beans and chickpeas – with a view to reducing the EU’s dependence on external imports and strengthening food security and the sustainability of Europe’s agri-food sector?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.2.2026) Given the persistent difficulties faced by protein crop production in the Union, particularly due to volatile local supply and demand and agronomic challenges, the Commission proposes, under the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy, to recognise the protein crop sector as a distinct sector for the purposes of the Common Market Organisation1.

The proposed mandatory recognition of producer and interbranch organisations will strengthen the value chain, and support for sectoral interventions will have to be offered in Member States where such organisations exist. The proposal will also allow for introducing marketing standards to better inform consumers about the products’ origin.

In the Commission’s Vision for Agriculture and Food2, the Commission underlines the need to develop a comprehensive plan to reduce the EU’s reliance on imported high-quality protein from a limited number of origins.

This initiative, due in second quarter of 2026, will focus in particular on fostering domestic production of plant protein with the aim of strengthening the EU’s food security and developing a more sustainable and resilient protein system. To this end, the Commission has proposed an increased ceiling for coupled income support that Member States may use to stimulate plant protein production on their territories.
